language_wrapper: In base 10, let P = '{pattern_p}' and Q = '{pattern_q}'. Among all integers n ≥ 2 with gcd(n, 10) = 1, determine the least n for which there exists an integer m with 1 ≤ m < n and gcd(m, n) = 1 such that the purely periodic decimal expansion of m/n contains both P and Q somewhere (not necessarily disjoint) in its fractional part. Moreover, there must exist indices i, j ≥ 1 (counting the first digit after the decimal point as position 1) such that the length-|P| block starting at i equals P and i ≡ {r1} (mod {t1}), and the length-|Q| block starting at j equals Q and j ≡ {r2} (mod {t2}). What is this least n?
hardness_rationale: This family strengthens the original problem in two coupled ways: (a) it requires two independent target blocks P and Q to appear in the same purely periodic decimal expansion of a reduced fraction m/n (with gcd(n,10)=1), and (b) it imposes simultaneous congruence constraints on the starting indices of these appearances modulo potentially unrelated moduli t1 and t2. Solving this in general requires a structural analysis of the long-division remainder dynamics rather than a single-block ad hoc construction. Proof sketch of correctness and the solver used by the verifier: For gcd(n,10)=1 the decimal expansion of m/n is purely periodic and the remainder sequence satisfies r_{k+1} = 10 r_k − d_k n with r_k ≡ 10^k m (mod n). For a fixed length-L digit block B with value Q_B, B appears starting at position k if and only if Q_B n ≤ 10^L r_k < (Q_B + 1) n; equivalently, r_k must lie in the integer interval [ceil(Q_B n / 10^L), floor(((Q_B + 1) n − 1)/10^L)]. Moreover, in a reduced expansion all remainders r_k are units modulo n, so we further require gcd(r_k, n) = 1. Thus the set S_B(n) of admissible starting remainders for block B is exactly the set of units r modulo n in that interval. Two blocks P and Q can occur in the same expansion for some m if and only if there exist r_P in S_P(n) and r_Q in S_Q(n) lying in the same coset of the cyclic subgroup ⟨10⟩ ⊆ (Z/nZ)^×, i.e., r_P ≡ 10^d r_Q (mod n) for some integer d. (Necessity: r_P ≡ 10^i m and r_Q ≡ 10^j m imply r_P r_Q^{−1} ≡ 10^{i−j}. Sufficiency: given such d one chooses i−j ≡ d (mod ord_n(10)) and a compatible m ≡ r_P · 10^{−i} ≡ r_Q · 10^{−j}.) The simultaneous index congruences i ≡ r1 (mod t1) and j ≡ r2 (mod t2) with the difference constraint i − j ≡ d (mod ord_n(10)) are solvable if and only if r1 − r2 − d ≡ 0 (mod gcd(t1, t2, ord_n(10))). This follows from the Chinese remainder theorem by eliminating i and requiring α ≡ j + d (mod gcd(t1, ord_n(10))) and then compatibility with j ≡ r2 (mod t2), yielding the modulus gcd(t1, t2, ord_n(10)). Therefore, for each n one need only: (1) compute ord_n(10) and the exponent table for ⟨10⟩, (2) compute S_P(n) and S_Q(n) via the interval criterion, (3) check for pairs (r_P, r_Q) with r_P r_Q^{−1} in ⟨10⟩ whose exponent d satisfies r1 − r2 − d ≡ 0 (mod gcd(t1, t2, ord_n(10))). The least n satisfying these conditions is exactly the answer. This analysis requires discrete log considerations within the 10-generated subgroup and compatibility of three congruences, which is conceptually and technically more involved than the original single-block existence problem.
notes: Implementation details: The verifier and generator both search n in ascending order, skipping n with gcd(n,10)≠1 to ensure purely periodic decimals. For each n, the multiplicative order ord_n(10) is found by looping powers until 1 reappears. The mapping of the 10-generated subgroup is recorded to allow constant-time discrete log queries. The admissible starting remainders for a block B are computed by the exact inequality window for r and filtered to units modulo n, which is necessary because only unit remainders occur in reduced expansions when gcd(n,10)=1. The simultaneous index congruence feasibility reduces to a single congruence modulo gcd(t1, t2, ord_n(10)), ensuring the difficulty is enforced by structure rather than brute-force search over numerators.
source_question: The decimal representation of $m/n,$ where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers and $m < n,$ contains the digits 2, 5, and 1 consecutively, and in that order. Find the smallest value of $n$ for which this is possible.
